title: Definition
body_md:
Let $B$ be a Boolean algebra. We define the \emph{internal} operators in
${\mathcal P} B$ as follows:
\begin{align*}
    \mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax} &= \set{0}, \\
    \mathord{\vphantom{\lnot}\mathpalette\ilnot@\relax} X &= \set{- a | a \in X},\\
    X \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} Y &= \set{a + b | a \in X, b \in Y}, \text{ and}\\
    X \mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax} Y &=\set{a \cdot b | a \in X, b \in Y},
\end{align*} where $X,Y \subseteq B$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The term algebra of formulas of LTP is denoted by $\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}$ and defined by the following grammar:
$$\varphi ::= \bot \mathrel| \mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax} \mathrel| P_i \mathrel| \lnot \varphi
\mathrel| \mathord{\vphantom{\lnot}\mathpalette\ilnot@\relax} \varphi \mathrel| \varphi \lor \varphi \mathrel| \varphi \land \varphi
\mathrel| \varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \varphi \mathrel| \varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax} \varphi. $$
head: environment

label: def_entailment
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def_entailment}
    Let $\Delta$ be a set of formulas. Then $\Delta \vDash \psi$ iff for all
    Boolean algebras $B$ and all homomorphisms $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$:
    $$\bigcap_{\varphi \in\Delta} H(\varphi) \subseteq H(\psi).$$
head: environment

label: def_satisfaction
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def_satisfaction}
    Let $B$ be a Boolean algebra, $v: \mathbb N \to {\mathcal P} B$ and $b\in B$. We define $B,v,b \vDash \varphi$ by the following recursive definition. 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $B,v,b \nvDash \bot$,
        \item $B,v, b \vDash P_i $ if $b \in v(i)$,
        \item $B,v,b \vDash \lnot \varphi$ if $B,v,b \nvDash \varphi$,
        \item $B,v,b \vDash \mathord{\vphantom{\lnot}\mathpalette\ilnot@\relax} \varphi$ if $B,v,- b \vDash \varphi$,
        \item $B,v,b \vDash \varphi \lor \psi$ if $B,v,b \vDash \varphi$ or  $B,v,b \vDash \psi$,
        \item $B,v,b \vDash \varphi \land \psi$ if $B,v,b \vDash \varphi$ and $B,v,b \vDash \psi$,
        \item $B,v,b \vDash \varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \psi$ if there are $b_1,b_2 \in B$ such that $b=b_1 + b_2$, $B,v,b_1 \vDash \varphi$ and  $B,v,b_2 \vDash \psi$, and
        \item $B,v,b \vDash \varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax} \psi$ if there are $b_1,b_2 \in B$ such that $b=b_1 \cdot b_2$, $B,v,b_1 \vDash \varphi$ and  $B,v,b_2 \vDash \psi$.
\end{itemize}
head: environment

label: prop:hom-sat-equivalence
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:hom-sat-equivalence}
Assume $B$ is a Boolean algebra, $v:\mathbb N \to {\mathcal P} B$, $b \in B$, and
$H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$ is a homomorphism such that $H(P_i)=v(i)$. Then
$B,v,b \vDash \varphi$ iff $b \in H(\varphi)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof proceeds by induction on $\varphi$.  The base case, where
$\varphi$ is $P_i$, is immediate: $b \in H(P_i)$ if and only if $b \in v
(i)$, which holds if and only if $B,v,b \vDash P_i$.

The inductive steps are routine. We illustrate one direction in the case where
$\varphi$ is $\psi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \delta$. Suppose that
$B,v,b \vDash \psi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \delta$. Then there exist $b_1, b_2 \in B$ such
that $b_1 + b_2 = b$, with $B,v,b_1 \vDash \psi$ and
$B,v,b_2 \vDash \delta$. By the inductive hypothesis, $b_1 \in H(\psi)$ and
$b_2 \in H(\delta)$, and hence $b = b_1 + b_2 \in H(\psi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \delta)$.
head: environment

label: prop:entailment-satisfaction-equivalence
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:entailment-satisfaction-equivalence}
$\Delta \vDash \psi$ iff for all Boolean algebras $B$, all
 $v : \mathbb N \to {\mathcal P} B$, and all $b \in B$, if $B,v,b \vDash \varphi$ for all
 $\varphi \in \Delta$, then $B,v,b \vDash \psi$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the left-to-right direction, assume that $\Delta \vDash \psi$, and let
$B$, $v$, and $b \in B$ be given. Suppose that $B,v,b \vDash \varphi$ for all
$\varphi \in \Delta$. Let $H : \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$ be the unique homomorphism such
that $H(P_i) = v(i)$ for each $i$. 
By Proposition~\ref{prop:hom-sat-equivalence}, $b \in H(\varphi)$ for all
$\varphi \in \Delta$, and hence, by Definition~\ref{def_entailment},
$b \in H(\psi)$. Applying Proposition~\ref{prop:hom-sat-equivalence} once more,
we conclude that $B,v,b \vDash \psi$.

The converse direction is proved similarly.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
If $\Delta \vDash \psi$ then $\sigma(\Delta) \vDash \sigma(\psi)$ for
    every algebra homomorphism $\sigma:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}$.
head: environment
name: Substitutionality

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows directly from the definitions, and the fact that if $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$
    is a homomorphism then so is $H\circ \sigma$.
head: environment

label: def:internal-top
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:internal-top}
The \emph{internal top} is the formula $\mathord{\vphantom{\top}\mathpalette\itop@\relax} := \mathord{\vphantom{\lnot}\mathpalette\ilnot@\relax}\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax}$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The term algebra of labels is denoted by $\ensuremath{\mathtt{Lb}}$ and defined by the following grammar:
$$\alpha ::= 0 \mathrel| p_i \mathrel| - \alpha \mathrel| \alpha + \alpha \mathrel|
\alpha \cdot \alpha.$$
The variables $p_i$ are called \emph{atomic labels}.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A \emph{labelled formula} is a pair of a label and a formula. We write a
labelled formula as $\alpha\mathbin: \varphi$ where $\alpha$ is the label and $\varphi$ the
formula.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\Gamma$ be a set of labelled formulas, then $ \Gamma \vDash \beta \mathbin: \psi$
    iff for all Boolean algebras $B$ and all homomorphisms $h: \ensuremath{\mathtt{Lb}} \to B$,
    $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$ if $h(\alpha) \in H(\varphi)$ for all $\alpha\mathbin: \varphi \in
    \Gamma$ then $h(\beta) \in H(\psi)$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
$\Delta \vDash \psi$ iff $p\mathbin: \Delta \vDash p\mathbin: \psi$, where $p$ is an atomic
    label and $p\mathbin: \Delta = \set{p\mathbin: \varphi | \varphi \in \Delta}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The left-to-right implication is immediate from the definitions. Assume
$p\mathbin: \Delta \vDash p\mathbin: \psi$, and let $b \in B$. We let $h: \ensuremath{\mathtt{Lb}} \to B$ be
such that $h(p)=b$, then by the assumption we know that if $b \in H
(\delta)$ for all $\delta \in \Delta$ then $b \in H(\psi)$. Thus, $\bigcap_
{\delta \in\Delta} H(\delta) \subseteq H(\psi)$.
head: environment

label: lem:basicfacts
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md:
Let $\Gamma$ be a set of labelled formulas and assume $\Gamma \vdash
\alpha \mathbin: \varphi$, then $\Gamma \vDash \alpha \mathbin: \varphi$.
head: environment
name: Soundness

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows from a straightforward induction on the construction of proof trees.
We will illustrate the proof with the case when the last rule of the proof
tree proving $\Gamma\vdash \beta \mathbin: \sigma$ is $\ensuremath{\mathord{\mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax}}\mathtt{E}}$: 
$$ \infer[\ensuremath{\mathord{\mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax}}\mathtt{E}}]{\beta\mathbin: \sigma}{\alpha \mathbin: \varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax} \psi & \infer*
{\beta \mathbin: \sigma}{\deduce{[\alpha =p\cdot q]}{\deduce{[q\mathbin: \psi]}{
[p\mathbin: \varphi]}}}}$$ 
The induction hypothesis gives us that $\Gamma \vDash \alpha \mathbin: \varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax} \psi $
and $\Gamma, p\mathbin: \varphi, q\mathbin: \psi ,\alpha =p\cdot q\vDash \beta \mathbin: \sigma$. If any
homomorphisms $H$ and $h$ make all labelled formulas in $\Gamma$ true then,
by the assumption, $h(\alpha) \in H(\varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax} \psi)$. This means that there are
$c \in H(\varphi)$ and $d \in H(\psi)$ such that $c\cdot d=h(\alpha)$. Let $h'$ be
the unique homomorphism that is like $h$ except that $h'(p)=c$ and $h'
(q)=d$. Then $h'$ and $H$ make $\Gamma$ true since $p$ and $q$ do not occur
in $\Gamma$. They also make $q\mathbin: \psi$ and $p\mathbin: \varphi $ true. Also, $h'
(\alpha  \leftrightarrow p\cdot q)= 1$ and so, they also make $\alpha =p\cdot q$
true. By the induction hypothesis this means that $h'$ and $H$ make
$\beta \mathbin: \sigma$ true. Now, since $p$ and $q$ do not occur in $\beta$ we can safely
conclude that $h$ and $H$ also make $\beta\mathbin: \sigma$ true.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: We say that $\Gamma$ is \emph{consistent} if $\Gamma \nvdash 0\mathbin: \bot$.
head: environment

label: prop:max
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: This follows directly from the $\ensuremath{\lnot\mathtt{I}}$ and $\ensuremath{\lnot\mathtt{E}}$ rules.
head: environment

label: prop:resp
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:resp}
If $\Gamma,\alpha \mathbin: \varphi\mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \psi$ is consistent and $p$ and $q$ are atomic
labels not occurring in $\Gamma$, nor in $\alpha $, then $\Gamma,
\alpha \mathbin: \varphi\mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \psi,p\mathbin: \varphi,q\mathbin: \psi,\alpha  = p + q$ is consistent. And
similarly for $\mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows directly from the $\ensuremath{\mathord{\mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax}}\mathtt{E}}$ rule, and the case for $\mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax}$ follows
in the same way from the $\ensuremath{\mathord{\mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax}}\mathtt{E}}$ rule.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
$\Gamma$ is \emph{$\mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax}$-saturated} if whenever $\alpha \mathbin: \varphi\mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax}
\psi \in \Gamma$ then there are labels $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ such that $\set{\beta_1\mathbin:
\varphi,\beta_2\mathbin: \psi,\alpha  = \beta_1 + \beta_2} \subseteq
\Gamma$. The dual notion of \emph{$\mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax}$-saturation} is defined similarly.
 We say that $\Gamma$ is \emph{saturated} if it is both $\mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax}$-saturated and
 $\mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax}$-saturated.
head: environment

title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
(1) If $\Gamma \vdash 0 \mathbin: \bot$ then the same derivation with all
 atomic labels renamed shows that $\Gamma' \vdash 0 \mathbin: \bot$. For the other
 direction we need to be a little bit more careful as a proof of $0 \mathbin: \bot$ may
 mention more atoms than those in $\Gamma'$. Let $\mathscr D$ be a derivation
 of $0 \mathbin: \bot$ from $\Gamma'$, and replace all atoms $p_{2i}$ by $p_i$ and all
 atoms $p_{2i+1}$ by $p_{i+k}$ where $k$ is large enough, i.e., larger than
 all indices of atoms occurring in $\mathscr D$. Then the resulting
 derivation shows that $\Gamma \vdash 0 \mathbin: \bot$.

(2) Given a Boolean algebra $B$ and homomorphisms $H$ and $h$ such that $h
(\alpha) \in H(\varphi)$ for all $\alpha:\varphi \in \Gamma$ we can define $h'$ by
setting $h'(p_{2i}) = h(p_i)$ and $h'(p_{2i+1}) = 0 \in B$. Then $B,H,h'$
satisfies $\Gamma'$. Also, if $B,H,h$ satisfies $\Gamma'$ then clearly for
$h'$ defined by $h'(p_{i})=h(p_{2i})$ we have that  $B,H,h'$ satisfies
$\Gamma$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: If $\Gamma \vDash \alpha \mathbin: \varphi$ then $\Gamma \vdash \alpha \mathbin: \varphi$.
head: environment
name: Completeness

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that $\Gamma \nvdash \alpha \mathbin: \varphi$. By Lemma \ref{lem:basicfacts} the
    set $\Gamma_0 =\Gamma,\alpha \mathbin: \lnot \varphi$ is consistent. We will extend it to
    a maximal consistent saturated set $\Gamma^\ast$. By applying the previous
    lemma we may assume that there are infinitely many atomic labels that
    are not mentioned in $\Gamma_0$.

    We construct $\Gamma^\ast$ as the union of $\Gamma_n$ where each
    $\Gamma_n$ is a finite extension of $\Gamma_0$. First, we enumerate all
    labelled formulas and when constructing $\Gamma_{n+1}$ we pick the $n$th
    labelled formula $\beta  \mathbin: \psi$ and add either $\beta \mathbin:\psi$ or
    $\beta \mathbin:\lnot\psi$. By Proposition \ref{prop:max} one of these is consistent
    with $\Gamma_n$.

    By Proposition \ref{prop:resp} we can assure that if we add a labelled
    formula $\beta \mathbin: \sigma \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \theta$ then we also add $p\mathbin: \sigma$, $q\mathbin:
    \theta$ and $\beta = p + q$ for some new atomic labels $p$ and
    $q$, and keeping $\Gamma_{n+1}$ consistent. 
    This construction assures that $\Gamma^\ast$ is maximal consistent and
    saturated.

    Now, let $T=\set{\alpha | \alpha \mathbin:  \mathord{\vphantom{\top}\mathpalette\itop@\relax} \in \Gamma^\ast}$. Let $B$ be the
    Lindenbaum--Tarski Boolean algebra of labels over $T$, i.e., its elements
    are equivalence classes of labels under the relation of $T$-provable
    equivalence: 
    \[
        B = \ensuremath{\mathtt{Lb}} / \mathord\sim_T = \set{[\alpha]_T | \alpha \in \ensuremath{\mathtt{Lb}}},
    \]
    where $\alpha  \sim_T b $ iff $T \vdash \alpha \leftrightarrow \beta $ (in classical
    propositional logic) and $[\alpha]_T=\set{\beta \in \ensuremath{\mathtt{Lb}} | \alpha \sim_T \beta}$. Observe
    that $B$ is the trivial one-element Boolean algebra iff $T$ is the
    inconsistent theory, i.e., iff $0 \in T$.
    Define the homomorphisms $h: \ensuremath{\mathtt{Lb}} \to B$  and $H: \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$ by
    \begin{gather*}
       h(p_i)=[p_i]_T \in B \text{ for atomic labels $p_i$, and}\\ H(P_i) = \set{h(\alpha) |
        \alpha\mathbin: P_i \in\Gamma^\ast} \text{ for atomic formulas $P_i$}.
    \end{gather*}

    {\sc Claim.} $h(\alpha) \in H(\varphi)$ iff $\alpha \mathbin: \varphi \in \Gamma^\ast$.

    The claim is proved by induction on formulas. The base case follows
    immediately from the definition of $H$ and the observation that 
    $$H(\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax}) =
    \{[0]_T\}. $$  This is seen by taking $h(\beta) \in H(\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax})$ and observing
    that $\beta \mathbin: \mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax}
    \in \Gamma^\ast$ and so $- \beta \mathbin: \mathord{\vphantom{\top}\mathpalette\itop@\relax}
    \in \Gamma^\ast$ and, thus, $- \beta  \in T$ and $\beta  \in [0]_T$.
    \begin{itemize}
        \item 
    If $\varphi$ is $\psi \lor \sigma$, $\psi \land \sigma$ or $\lnot \psi$
    the induction step is straightforward, as for example $\alpha  \mathbin:  \psi \land
    \sigma \in \Gamma^\ast$ iff $\alpha \mathbin: \psi \in \Gamma^\ast$ and $\alpha \mathbin: \sigma
    \in \Gamma^\ast$ and, by the induction hypothesis, this is equivalent to
    $h(\alpha ) \in H(\psi)$ and $h(\alpha ) \in H(\sigma)$, i.e., $h(\alpha ) \in H(\psi) \cap
    H(\sigma) = H(\psi\land \sigma)$.

\item 
    For the case when $\varphi$ is $\mathord{\vphantom{\lnot}\mathpalette\ilnot@\relax} \psi$ note that $\alpha \mathbin:  \mathord{\vphantom{\lnot}\mathpalette\ilnot@\relax} \psi
    \in \Gamma^\ast$ iff $- \alpha  \mathbin: \psi \in \Gamma^\ast$ iff $h(- \alpha )
    \in H(\psi)$ iff $- h(\alpha ) \in H(\psi)$ iff $h(\alpha) \in H(\mathord{\vphantom{\lnot}\mathpalette\ilnot@\relax} \psi)$.

\item 
    When $\varphi$ is $\psi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \sigma$ note that $\alpha \mathbin:  \psi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \sigma \in
    \Gamma^\ast$ iff there are labels $\beta_1 $ and $\beta_2$ such that $\beta_1 \mathbin: \psi \in
    \Gamma^\ast$, $\beta_2\mathbin: \sigma \in \Gamma^\ast$ and $\alpha = \beta_1 +
    \beta_2 \in \Gamma^\ast$. By the induction hypothesis this is
    equivalent to $h(\beta_1) \in H(\psi)$, $h(\beta_2) \in H(\sigma)$ and $h(\alpha) = h(\beta_1+
    \beta_2) = h(\beta_1) + h(\beta_2)$. Thus this is equivalent to $h(\alpha) \in H(\psi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax}
    \sigma)$.
\item 
    The case when $\varphi$ is $\psi \mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax} \sigma$ is treated similarly, ending the proof of the claim.
\end{itemize}
    It now follows immediately that for these choices
    of $B$, $H$, and $h$ we have $h(\alpha) \in H(\varphi)$ for all $\alpha \mathbin:\varphi \in
    \Gamma_0$ and thus $\Gamma \nvDash \alpha \mathbin:\varphi$.

title: Corollary
body_md: The logic LTP is compact.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
This follows directly from soundness and completeness with respect to a finitary proof
system.

title: Definition
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A class $\mathcal{X}$ of Boolean algebras is \emph{adequate} for LTP if
    for every $\Delta$ and $\psi$ we have
    \[
    \Delta \vDash \psi \text{ iff } \Delta \vDash_\mathcal{X} \psi.
    \] 
   A single Boolean algebra $B$ is said to be \emph{canonical} for LTP if $\set{B}$
    is adequate for LTP.
head: environment

label: lemma:trivial
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item     $\vDash_B \mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax}$ means that $B=\{0\}$ and thus that $B=\mathbbm 1$.
    \item Let $H$ be any homomorphism, then $H(\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax} \lor \mathord{\vphantom{\lnot}\mathpalette\ilnot@\relax}\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax})=\{0\} \cup  \{1\}$ which is $B$ iff $B\in \{ \mathbbm 1,\mathbbm 2 \}$.
    \item  Since $\varphi$ contains no propositional variables, $H(\varphi)=H'(\varphi)$ for all homomorphisms $H,H': \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$. 
    Let $H$ be any such homomorphism. 

    If $\vDash_B\varphi$ then $H(\lnot \varphi)=\emptyset$, and $H(\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax} \mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax}\lnot \varphi)=\emptyset$. 
    Thus, $H(\lnot \mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax} \lor (\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax} \mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax} \lnot \varphi) )=H(\lnot \mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax})\neq B$. 
    On the other hand, if $\nvDash_B\varphi$ then  $H(\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax} \mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax}\lnot \varphi)=\{0\}$, and 
    thus, $H(\lnot \mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax} \lor (\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax} \mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax} \lnot \varphi) )= (B\setminus \{0\}) \cup \{0\} = B$.\qedhere
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: No Boolean algebra is canonical for LTP.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It follows from Lemma \ref{lemma:trivial} that there are formulas $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$ such
that $\vDash_B \varphi_1$ iff $B\neq \mathbbm 1$ and $\vDash_B \varphi_2$ iff
$B\neq \mathbbm 2$. This means that for any class of Boolean algebras $\mathcal
{X}$, if $\mathbbm 1 \notin \mathcal{X}$ then $\vDash_\mathcal{X} \varphi_1$. However,
$\nvDash \varphi_1$, and thus for $\mathcal{X}$ to be adequate we must have that
$\mathbbm 1 \in \mathcal{X}$. Similarly for $\varphi_2$ and $\mathbbm 2$ and thus, any
adequate set $X$ includes both $\mathbbm 1$ and $\mathbbm 2$.
head: environment

title: Theorem
body_md: The class of countable (including finite) Boolean algebras is adequate for LTP.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof of the completeness theorem constructs a Boolean algebra $B$ as a
Lindenbaum--Tarski algebra over a countably infinite set of propositional
variables. More precisely, suppose that $\Delta \nvDash \varphi$. Then
$p\mathbin: \Delta \nvDash p\mathbin:\varphi$ and, hence, by soundness $p\mathbin: \Delta \nvdash
p\mathbin:\varphi$. By the proof of the completeness theorem, there is a finite or
countable Boolean algebra $B$, and homomorphisms $h: \ensuremath{\mathtt{Lb}} \to B$ and
$H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$ such that $h(p) \in H(\psi)$ for all $\psi \in \Delta$ and
$h(p) \notin H(\varphi)$. Thus, $$\bigcap_{\psi \in \Delta} H(\psi) \nsubseteq H
(\varphi)$$ and therefore $ \Delta \nvDash_{\{B\}} \varphi$.

title: Definition
head: environment

label: th:deduction
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Deduction theorem for LTP

title: Proof
body_md:
By the definition of external implication we have, for every Boolean algebra
	$B$ and every homomorphism $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$,
	$$H(\varphi \to \psi)=H(\lnot\varphi \lor \psi)=\bigl(B\setminus H(\varphi)\bigr)\cup H(\psi).$$
	Assume first that $\Delta,\varphi \vDash \psi$, and let
	$b\in \bigcap_{\delta\in\Delta} H(\delta)$. If $b\notin H(\varphi)$, then
	$b\in H(\lnot\varphi)$, and hence $b\in H(\varphi\to\psi)$. If instead
	$b\in H(\varphi)$, then by the assumption $b\in H(\psi)$, and again
	$b\in H(\varphi\to\psi)$. Thus $\Delta\vDash \varphi\to\psi$.

	Conversely, assume that $\Delta\vDash \varphi\to\psi$, and let
	$b\in \bigcap_{\delta\in\Delta}H(\delta)\cap H(\varphi)$. By the assumption,
	$b\in H(\varphi\to\psi)$. Since $b\in H(\varphi)$, we have
	$b\notin H(\lnot\varphi)$, so $b\in H(\psi)$. Hence
	$\Delta,\varphi\vDash \psi$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The constants $\top$ and $\mathord{\text{NB}}$ are defined by
	\[
		\top := \lnot\bot
		\quad\text{and}\quad
		\mathord{\text{NB}} :=\lnot \mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax}.
	\]
head: environment

label: prop:constant_semantics
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:constant_semantics}
	For every Boolean algebra $B$ and every homomorphism $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}\to{\mathcal P} B$,
	\[
		H(\top)=B,
		\qquad
		H(\mathord{\text{NB}})=\set{x\in B \mid x\neq0},\qquad\text{and}
		\qquad
		H(\mathord{\vphantom{\top}\mathpalette\itop@\relax})=\set{1}.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $H(\bot)=\emptyset$, the first equality follows from the external
	interpretation of $\lnot$. Since $H(\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax})=\set{0}$, the second equality
	follows in the same way. Finally, since $\mathord{\vphantom{\top}\mathpalette\itop@\relax}=\mathord{\vphantom{\lnot}\mathpalette\ilnot@\relax}\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax}$ and the internal
	negation is interpreted pointwise, $H(\mathord{\vphantom{\top}\mathpalette\itop@\relax})=\set{-0}=\set{1}$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The \emph{downward-closure} and \emph{upward-closure} operators are defined
	by
	\[
		\mathop{\downarrow} \varphi := \varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax} \top
		\quad\text{and}\quad
		\mathop{\uparrow} \varphi := \varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \top.
	\]
For elements $a$ and $b$ of a Boolean algebra, we write $a\leq b$ for the
Boolean algebra order, i.e., $a\cdot b=a$.
head: environment

label: prop:closure_semantics
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:closure_semantics}
	For every Boolean algebra $B$, every homomorphism $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}\to{\mathcal P} B$, and every
	$\varphi\in\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}$,
	\[
		H(\mathop{\downarrow}\varphi)=\set{b\in B\mid \text{there exists }a\in H(\varphi)\text{ such that }b\leq a},
	\]
	and
	\[
		H(\mathop{\uparrow}\varphi)=\set{b\in B\mid \text{there exists }a\in H(\varphi)\text{ such that }a\leq b}.
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition \ref{prop:constant_semantics}, $H(\top)=B$. Hence
	\[
		H(\mathop{\downarrow}\varphi)=H(\varphi\mathrel{\vphantom{\land}\mathpalette\iland@\relax}\top)=
		\set{a\cdot c\mid a\in H(\varphi), c\in B}.
	\]
	This is exactly the set of elements below some element of $H(\varphi)$. The
	argument for $\mathop{\uparrow}$ is the same, replacing meet by join.
head: environment

label: prop:closure_properties
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:closure_properties}
	For every Boolean algebra $B$, every homomorphism $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}\to{\mathcal P} B$, and every
	$\varphi\in\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}$, the following hold:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $H(\mathop{\downarrow}\mathop{\downarrow}\varphi)=H(\mathop{\downarrow}\varphi)$ and $H(\mathop{\uparrow}\mathop{\uparrow}\varphi)=H(\mathop{\uparrow}\varphi)$.
		\item $H(\mathop{\downarrow}\varphi)=\emptyset$ iff $H(\varphi)=\emptyset$, and otherwise
		$0\in H(\mathop{\downarrow}\varphi)$.
		\item $H(\mathop{\uparrow}\varphi)=\emptyset$ iff $H(\varphi)=\emptyset$, and otherwise
		$1\in H(\mathop{\uparrow}\varphi)$.
		\item $H(\mathop{\downarrow}\varphi)=B$ iff $1\in H(\varphi)$.
		\item $H(\mathop{\uparrow}\varphi)=B$ iff $0\in H(\varphi)$.
	\end{enumerate}
	Moreover, $\top$ and $\bot$ are the only common fix-points of the two
	operators.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first five statements follow immediately from Proposition
	\ref{prop:closure_semantics}. For example, if $H(\varphi)$ is non-empty and
	$a\in H(\varphi)$, then $0\leq a$, so $0\in H(\mathop{\downarrow}\varphi)$; and
	$H(\mathop{\downarrow}\varphi)=B$ holds exactly when every element is below some element of
	$H(\varphi)$, which in a Boolean algebra is equivalent to $1\in H(\varphi)$.
	The remaining cases are similar.

	If $A\subseteq B$ is both downward- and upward-closed and non-empty,
	then from any $a\in A$ we get both $0\in A$ and $1\in A$, and hence
	$A=B$. Thus the only common fix-points are $\emptyset$ and $B$, i.e. the
	interpretations of $\bot$ and $\top$.
head: environment

label: def:modal-operators
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:modal-operators}
	The modal operators $\mathord{\vphantom{\Box}\mathpalette\dBox@\relax}$ and $\Box$ are defined by 
	\[
		\mathord{\vphantom{\Box}\mathpalette\dBox@\relax} \varphi := \lnot\mathop{\downarrow}\lnot\varphi 
		\quad\text{and}\quad
		\Box \varphi := \lnot \mathop{\uparrow} \mathop{\downarrow} \lnot \varphi.
	\]
head: environment

label: prop:modal_semantics
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:modal_semantics}
	For every Boolean algebra $B$, every homomorphism $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}\to{\mathcal P} B$, and every
	$\varphi\in\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}$,
	\[
		H(\mathord{\vphantom{\Box}\mathpalette\dBox@\relax}\varphi)=\set{a\in B\mid \text{for all } b\geq a,\ b\in H(\varphi)}.
	\]
	Moreover, $H(\Box\varphi)=B$ if $H(\varphi)=B$, and $H(\Box\varphi)=\emptyset$
	otherwise.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By the definition of $\mathord{\vphantom{\Box}\mathpalette\dBox@\relax}$ and Proposition \ref{prop:closure_semantics}:
	$a\in H(\mathord{\vphantom{\Box}\mathpalette\dBox@\relax}\varphi)$ iff $a\notin H(\mathop{\downarrow}\lnot\varphi)$. This holds iff there is no
	$b\in B\setminus H(\varphi)$ such that $a\leq b$, which is equivalent to saying
	that every $b\geq a$ belongs to $H(\varphi)$.

	For $\Box$, observe first that $H(\mathop{\downarrow}\lnot\varphi)=\emptyset$ iff
	$H(\lnot\varphi)=\emptyset$, iff $H(\varphi)=B$. In that case
	$H(\mathop{\uparrow}\mathop{\downarrow}\lnot\varphi)=\emptyset$, and hence $H(\Box\varphi)=B$. If instead
	$H(\varphi)\neq B$, then $H(\lnot\varphi)$ is non-empty, so by Proposition
	\ref{prop:closure_properties}, $H(\mathop{\uparrow}\mathop{\downarrow}\lnot\varphi)=B$. Hence
	$H(\Box\varphi)=\emptyset$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $B$ be a Boolean algebra, let $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}\to{\mathcal P} B$ be a homomorphism, and let
	$a\in B$. The relation $B,H,a\Vdash\varphi$ is the usual modal satisfaction
	relation in the Kripke model whose set of worlds is $B$, whose accessibility
	relation for $\mathord{\vphantom{\Box}\mathpalette\dBox@\relax}$ is the order $\leq$ of $B$, and whose accessibility
	relation for $\Box$ is the universal relation on $B$. Thus
	\[
		B,H,a\Vdash P_i \quad\text{iff}\quad a\in H(P_i),
	\]
	and the Boolean connectives are interpreted by the standard clauses:
	                                  
	\begin{align*}
		B,H,a \nVdash \bot \phantom{soii} \\
		B,H,a\Vdash \lnot\varphi \phantom{sii}&\quad\text{iff}\quad B,H,a\nVdash\varphi,\\
		B,H,a\Vdash\varphi\land\psi &\quad\text{iff}\quad B,H,a\Vdash\varphi
			\text{ and } B,H,a\Vdash\psi,\\
		B,H,a\Vdash\varphi\lor\psi &\quad\text{iff}\quad B,H,a\Vdash\varphi
			\text{ or } B,H,a\Vdash\psi.\\
		B,H,a\Vdash\varphi\to\psi &\quad\text{iff}\quad B,H,a\nVdash\varphi
			\text{ or } B,H,a\Vdash\psi.
	\end{align*}
	Moreover,
	\begin{align*}
		B,H,a\Vdash\mathord{\vphantom{\Box}\mathpalette\dBox@\relax}\varphi &\quad\text{iff}\quad
			B,H,b\Vdash\varphi\text{ for all }b\in B\text{ such that }a\leq b,\\
		B,H,a\Vdash\Box\varphi &\quad\text{iff}\quad
			B,H,b\Vdash\varphi\text{ for all }b\in B.
	\end{align*}
head: environment

label: prop:modal
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:modal}
	If $\varphi$ is a formula in the language of modal logic with the two modal box
	operators, i.e., a formula built up from atoms using
	$\bot,\lnot,\land,\lor,\to,\mathord{\vphantom{\Box}\mathpalette\dBox@\relax},$ and $\Box$; $B$ is a Boolean algebra and $H$ a
	homomorphism $\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$, then
	\[
		B,H,a \Vdash \varphi \quad\text{iff}\quad a \in H(\varphi).
	\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The proof is by induction on $\varphi$. The Boolean cases are immediate from
	the interpretation of the external Boolean connectives. The case for $\mathord{\vphantom{\Box}\mathpalette\dBox@\relax}$
	is Proposition \ref{prop:modal_semantics}. The case for $\Box$ follows from
	the second part of Proposition \ref{prop:modal_semantics}, since $\Box$ is
	interpreted as the universal necessity operator.
head: environment

label: prop:S5_fragment
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition \ref{prop:modal_semantics}, $\Box$ is interpreted as the
universal modality. Thus every LTP interpretation gives a universal Kripke model,
with the elements of the underlying Boolean algebra as worlds.

Conversely, if a formula in this fragment is not valid in S5, then it fails in
some finite universal Kripke model. By adding copies of worlds with the same
valuation, if necessary, we may assume that the number of worlds is the
cardinality of some finite Boolean algebra. Such duplication does not affect
truth of formulas in the $\Box$-fragment. We may therefore identify the worlds
with the elements of that Boolean algebra, obtaining an LTP countermodel.
Hence the validities of this fragment are precisely the validities of universal
Kripke frames, i.e., S5.
head: environment

label: thm:finite_ba
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:finite_ba}
	The set of finite Boolean algebras is not adequate for LTP.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The following formula called \emph{Grzegorczyk's formula}
	\[
		\text{Grz:}\quad\mathord{\vphantom{\Box}\mathpalette\dBox@\relax}(\mathord{\vphantom{\Box}\mathpalette\dBox@\relax}(P\to \mathord{\vphantom{\Box}\mathpalette\dBox@\relax} P)\to P)\to P
	\]
	is known to be valid on all finite partially ordered Kripke frames, see \cite{Bull1984}.
	Thus, by Proposition \ref{prop:modal}, $\vDash_B \text{Grz}$ for all finite
	Boolean algebras $B$.

	On the other hand, if $B={\mathcal P} \mathbb N$ and $H: \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$ is such that
	$H(P)=B \setminus \{\emptyset,\{0,1\},\{0,1,2,3\},\ldots\}$, it is a
	straightforward calculation to check that $H(\text{Grz})=H(P) \neq B$.
	Therefore, $\nvDash_{{\mathcal P} {\mathbb N}} \text{Grz}$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
For a subset $A$ and an element $b$ of a Boolean algebra $B$ we say that $b$
	is \emph{separate} from $A$ if for all $a \in A$, $b\cdot a = 0$. We
	define $\mathord{{\sim}} A$ as the set of all elements separate from $A$, i.e.,
	$$\mathord{{\sim}} A = \set{ b \in B | \text{for all } a\in A, b\cdot a = 0 }.$$
head: environment

label: strict_negation
title: Definition
head: environment

label: slnot_form_to_subset
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first convince ourselves that for any algebra, homomorphism and formula
	as prescribed we have
	$$H(\mathop{\downarrow} \varphi \land \mathord{\text{NB}})= \set{ a \in  B |  a \neq 0 \text{ and } a\leq b
	\text{ for some } b\in H(\varphi)}.$$
	Therefore $H(\mathop{\uparrow}(\mathop{\downarrow} \varphi \land \mathord{\text{NB}}))$ is the set of elements of $B$ that
	have non-trivial intersection with some element in $H(\varphi)$, i.e.,
	$$H(\mathop{\uparrow} (\mathop{\downarrow} \varphi \land \mathord{\text{NB}}))= \set{ a\in B | a\cdot b \neq 0 \text{ for
	some } b\in H(\varphi)}.$$
	This is exactly the complement of $\mathord{{\sim}} H(\varphi)$, and thus $
	H(\mathord{{\sim}}\varphi)=  H (\lnot\mathop{\uparrow}( \mathop{\downarrow} \varphi\land \mathord{\text{NB}} ))= \mathord{{\sim}} H(\varphi)$.
head: environment

label: prop_strict_neg
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For a semantic proof of (1) we need to show that for any Boolean algebra $B$ and
any $A\subseteq B$ we have that $A\subseteq \mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} A$. In other words, if
$a\in A$ then for all $b\in \mathord{{\sim}} A$ we have that $a\cdot b= 0$, which is
guaranteed by the definition of $\mathord{{\sim}} A$. 

As a simple proof of statement (2), consider for any Boolean algebra a
homomorphism $H$ such that $H(P)= \emptyset$. Then $H(\mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} P) =
\set{0}$. Clearly then $H(\mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} P)\nsubseteq H( P)$ and the
statement is proved.

For (3) assume for some $A\subseteq B $ that $b \in \mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} A$.
Then for all $a\in A$, by the semantic proof of (1) we have that $a\in\mathord{{\sim}}
\mathord{{\sim}} A$, and thus $b\cdot a = 0$, and thus $b\in \mathord{{\sim}} A$. Hence $\mathord{{\sim}}
\mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} A \subseteq \mathord{{\sim}} A$. This proves statement (3).

For (4) let $B$ be the four element Boolean algebra $\{0,a,b,1\}$ and $A=\{0,a,b\}$. Then $\mathord{{\sim}} A =\{0\}$ and $A \cup \mathord{{\sim}} A = A \neq B$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $B$ be a Boolean algebra and $H$ a homomorphism $\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$. We
	define the \emph{local entailment} of $H$ denoted $\Delta \vDash_H \varphi $ for LTP-formulas in
	the expected way:
	$$\Delta \vDash_H \varphi \quad \text{ iff } \quad
	\bigcap_{\delta\in \Delta} H(\delta) \subseteq H(\varphi).$$
	Given a class of homomorphisms $\mathcal{H}$ (not necessarily all to the
	same algebra), we define the corresponding entailment relation $$
	\Delta \vDash_{\mathcal H} \varphi \quad \text{iff}\quad\text{for all }  H\in
	\mathcal{H}, \Delta \vDash_H \varphi.$$
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
A class of homomorphisms $\mathcal{H}$ is \textit{definable} in LTP if there
	exists a set of formulas $\Pi$ such that for all homomorphisms $H: \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to
	{\mathcal P} B$,
	$$H\in \mathcal{H} \quad \text{iff } \quad \vDash_H \pi \text{
		for all } \pi \in \Pi. $$
head: environment

label: Def_to_ax
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{Def_to_ax}
	Assume a class of homomorphisms $\mathcal{H}$ is defined by a set of formulas
	$\Pi$ and let $\Box\Pi= \set{\Box \pi | \pi\in \Pi}$. Then 
	$$ \Delta, \Box \Pi \vDash \varphi \quad \text{ iff } \quad
\Delta \vDash_{\mathcal H} \varphi.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume first that $\Delta, \Box\Pi \vDash \varphi$. Let
	$H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}\to {\mathcal P} B$ be a homomorphism in $\mathcal{H}$, and suppose that
	$b\in \bigcap_{\delta\in\Delta} H(\delta)$. Since $\mathcal{H}$ is defined
	by $\Pi$, we have $\vDash_H \pi$ for every $\pi\in\Pi$, that is,
	$H(\pi)=B$. Hence, by the semantics of $\Box$, we have
	$H(\Box\pi)=B$ for every $\pi\in\Pi$. It follows that
	\[
		b\in \bigcap_{\delta\in\Delta} H(\delta)
		\cap
		\bigcap_{\pi\in\Pi} H(\Box\pi).
	\]
	By the assumption $\Delta,\Box\Pi\vDash \varphi$, we conclude that
	$b\in H(\varphi)$. Thus $\Delta\vDash_H\varphi$. Since $H\in\mathcal{H}$ was
	arbitrary, $\Delta\vDash_{\mathcal{H}}\varphi$.

	Conversely, assume that $\Delta\vDash_{\mathcal{H}}\varphi$. Let
	$H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}\to {\mathcal P} B$ be any homomorphism, and suppose that
	\[
		b\in \bigcap_{\delta\in\Delta} H(\delta)
		\cap
		\bigcap_{\pi\in\Pi} H(\Box\pi).
	\]
	Then $H(\Box\pi)$ is non-empty for every $\pi\in\Pi$. Since, for every
	formula $\eta$, the set $H(\Box\eta)$ is either $B$ or $\emptyset$, it
	follows that $H(\Box\pi)=B$ for every $\pi\in\Pi$. Hence $H(\pi)=B$ for
	every $\pi\in\Pi$, i.e. $\vDash_H\pi$ for every $\pi\in\Pi$. Since
	$\Pi$ defines $\mathcal{H}$, this means that $H\in\mathcal{H}$. By
	$\Delta\vDash_{\mathcal{H}}\varphi$, we therefore have
	$\Delta\vDash_H\varphi$, and since $b\in\bigcap_{\delta\in\Delta}H(\delta)$,
	we get $b\in H(\varphi)$. Thus $\Delta,\Box\Pi\vDash\varphi$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\Delta\cup \set{\psi}\subseteq \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}$. Then $\Delta \vDash^\top \psi$
	iff for all Boolean algebras  $B$ and all homomorphisms $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$:
	if $H(\delta)= H(\top)$ for all $\delta \in \Delta$ then $H(\psi)= H
	(\top)$. We denote this logic by $\text{LTP}^\top$, the \emph
	{assertional companion of} LTP.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md:
For all LTP-formulas $\varphi$ and $\psi$, $\Box \varphi \vDash \psi$ iff for
	every Boolean algebra $B$ and every homomorphism $H : \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$, $H
	(\varphi)=H(\top)$ implies $H(\psi)=H(\top)$. Consequently, for $\text
	{LTP}^\top$: $$\varphi \vDash^\top \psi \text{  if and only
	if } \vDash^\top \Box \varphi \to \psi.$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $H(\top)=B$, and $H(\Box\varphi)=B$ iff $H(\varphi)=B$, the statement
  $\Box\varphi \vDash \psi$ says exactly that, for every Boolean algebra $B$
  and every homomorphism $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}\to{\mathcal P} B$, if $H(\varphi)=H(\top)$, then $H
  (\psi)=H(\top)$. The consequently part then follows from the deduction
  theorem of LTP (Theorem \ref{th:deduction}) and the clear fact that LTP and
  $\text{LTP}^\top$ have the same theorems.
head: environment

label: def:PTplus
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:PTplus}
The set of formulas $\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}_{\text{PT}^+}$ of \emph{strong propositional team logic},
$\text{PT}^+$,  is generated by the following grammar $$ \varphi::= P_i
\mathrel|  \mathord{{\sim}} P_i \mathrel|\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax} \mathrel| \mathord{\text{NB}}\mathrel|
\varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \varphi\mathrel|   \varphi \land \varphi \mathrel|  \varphi \lor \varphi $$ and
its valuational team semantics can be described by defining the denotations
for formulas $\llbracket  \varphi  \rrbracket_{} \subseteq {\mathcal P} 2^\mathbb{N} $
recursively for cases of the main connective as follows:
\begin{align*}
	\llbracket   P_i  \rrbracket_{} &= \set{ X | \text {for all } s \in X, s(i)= 1}\\
	\llbracket  \mathord{{\sim}} P_i  \rrbracket_{} &= \set{ X | \text {for all } s \in X, s(i)= 0}\\
	\llbracket  \mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax}  \rrbracket_{} &= \set{ \emptyset}\\
	\llbracket  \mathord{\text{NB}}  \rrbracket_{} &= \set {X| X\neq \emptyset} \\
	\llbracket  \varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \psi  \rrbracket_{} &= \set{ X\cup Y | X\in \llbracket 
	\varphi  \rrbracket_{}, Y\in \llbracket  \psi  \rrbracket_{}} \\
	\llbracket  \varphi \land \psi  \rrbracket_{} &= \llbracket  \varphi  \rrbracket_{} \cap
	\llbracket  \psi  \rrbracket_{}\\
	\llbracket  \varphi \lor \psi  \rrbracket_{} &= \llbracket  \varphi  \rrbracket_{} \cup
	\llbracket  \psi  \rrbracket_{}\\
\end{align*}
The logical entailment of $\text{PT}^+$ is then defined as follows:
$$\Delta \vDash_{\text{PT}^+} \varphi \quad \text{iff} \quad
\bigcap_{\delta \in \Delta}  \llbracket  \delta  \rrbracket_{} \subseteq \llbracket 
\varphi  \rrbracket_{}.$$
Elements $s\in 2^\mathbb{N}$ are viewed as \textit{valuations} for the set of
propositional variables, and sets of valuations $X\in {\mathcal P} 2^\mathbb{N}$ are
referred to as \textit{teams (of valuations)}.
head: environment

title: Definition
head: environment

label: directThm
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{directThm}
	For all formulas $\Delta\cup \{\varphi\} \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}_{\mathrm{PT}^+}$:
	\[
		 \Delta \vDash_{\mathrm{PT}^+} \varphi \quad \text{ iff } \quad \Delta \vDash_{H_V} \varphi.
	\]
head: environment

label: excluded_middle
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{excluded_middle} 
	For all Boolean algebras $B$, all homomorphisms $ H: \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$, and all
	formulas $\varphi \in \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}$ we have $$ \vDash_H \varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \mathord{{\sim}} \varphi
	\quad \text{iff}\quad H(\varphi) \text{ is a principal ideal} $$
head: environment

label: negated_principal
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{negated_principal}
	For a Boolean algebra $B$, if $A\subseteq B$ is a principal ideal with
	maximal element $a\in B$, then $\mathord{{\sim}} A$ is a principal ideal with
	maximal element $- a$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First note that for all $A\subseteq B$ we have that $\mathord{{\sim}} A$ is downward-closed, 
since if $c\leq c'\in \mathord{{\sim}} A$ then for all $b\in A$, $ b\cdot c \leq
b\cdot c' = 0$. What is left to show is that, if $a= \bigvee A$, then
$- a = \bigvee \mathord{{\sim}} A$. 

Clearly, for all $a'\in A$ we have $a'\cdot a = a'$. Hence
\[		
	- a \cdot a'=- a \cdot (a'\cdot a)=	a'\cdot(- a\cdot a)	=0,
\]
and therefore $- a\in \mathord{{\sim}} A$. 
Furthermore, if $b\in \mathord{{\sim}} A$,
then $a\cdot b = 0$ and therefore $- a = - a +
(a \cdot b)= - a + b$, i.e., $b\leq
- a$. Thus, $- a $ is an upper bound of $ \mathord{{\sim}} A$ included in
the set, and therefore the set is a principal ideal, and $- a = \bigvee
\mathord{{\sim}} A$.
head: environment
name: Proof of Lemma \ref{negated_principal}

title: Proof
body_md:
For one direction, assume $H(\varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \mathord{{\sim}} \varphi)= B$, we then need to
prove that  $H(\varphi)$ is a principal ideal. First we establish that it is
downward-closed.  In search of a contradiction, assume that for some $a\in H
(\varphi)$ we can find $b\in B$ such that $b\leq a$ and $b\notin H(\varphi)$. We
want to show that then $b\notin H(\varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \mathord{{\sim}}
\varphi)$. If $b\in H(\varphi\mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \mathord{{\sim}} \varphi)$, then there exists $c\in H(\varphi)$
and $d \in \mathord{{\sim}} H(\varphi)$ such that $c+ d= b $. Since $b\leq a \in
H(\varphi)$ we have that $$ b\cdot d \leq a\cdot d = 0$$ since $d\in
\mathord{{\sim}} H(\varphi)$. But then, since clearly $c\leq b$, we have $$b= b\cdot b
= (c+ d ) \cdot b = ( c\cdot b )+ (b\cdot d)= c\in H(\varphi)$$ This is a
contradiction. We can therefore conclude, under the main assumption, that
$H(\varphi)$ is downward-closed. Next we show that $\bigvee H(\varphi)\in H(\varphi)$.
By assumption we have that  $$1 \in H(\varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \mathord{{\sim}}
\varphi)$$ Then there exists $c \in  H(\varphi)$ and $d \in H(\mathord{{\sim}} \varphi )$ such
that $c+ d=1$. Furthermore, for all $a \in H(\varphi)$ we have that $$a =
1 \cdot a = (c+ d) \cdot a = c \cdot a, $$ since $d \cdot a  =
0$ for all $a \in H( \varphi) $. Consequently $a \leq c $ for all $a
\in H( \varphi)$ and thus $ c$ is an upper bound for $H(\varphi)$ included in
the set, i.e. $c  = \bigvee H(\varphi)$. With downward closure established, this
also means that $H(\varphi)$ is a principal ideal.
	
	
For the other direction, assume $H(\varphi)$ is a principal ideal. Then there
exists $a \in B$ such that $a$ is the top element of $H(\varphi)$. Then by Lemma
\ref{negated_principal} we see that  $- a$ is the top element of the
principal ideal $H(\mathord{{\sim}} \varphi)$. Therefore, since $a + - a =
1$ we have for every $b\in B$ that $$b= b \cdot (a+ - a)= (b\cdot a )
+ (b\cdot - a).$$ Being the top elements of the respective principal
ideals we observe that $$b\cdot a \in  H(\varphi)\quad \text{and} \quad b
\cdot - a \in H(\mathord{{\sim}} \varphi)$$ and conclude that  $ H(\varphi  \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax}
\mathord{{\sim}} \varphi)= B$, in other words $H\vDash \varphi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \mathord{{\sim}} \varphi$.
head: environment
name: Proof of Theorem \ref{excluded_middle}

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\mathcal{H}_{\text{PV}}$ denote the class of homomorphisms defined by
	$$\set{ P_i\mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \mathord{{\sim}} P_i | i\in \mathbb{N}}.$$ We say that a
	homomorphism $H$ \textit{has principal  variables} iff
	$H\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{PV}}$. Furthermore, let \emph{the principal variable
	axioms} be the set
	\[
	\text{PVA}=\set{\Box ( P_i \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \mathord{{\sim}} P_i) |i\in	\mathbb{N}}.
	\]

label: thm:mainAx
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:mainAx}
	For all $\Delta \cup \{ \varphi \} \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}_{\mathrm{PT}^+}$ 
	\[ 
	\Delta \vDash_{\mathrm{PT}^+} \varphi \quad \text{iff} \quad \mathrm{PVA}, \Delta \vDash \varphi.
	\]

label: thm:completeBA
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:completeBA}
	Every Boolean algebra can be embedded into a complete atomic Boolean
	algebra of the form $({\mathcal P} S, \emptyset, \cdot^C, \cup, \cap)$ for some set
	$S$.

title: Definition
body_md:
In a Boolean algebra $B$, if $a,b\in B$ and $a\leq b$, then let
		$[a,b]\subseteq B$ denote the set of elements between $a$ and $b$,
		that is $$[a,b]= \set{c\in B | a\leq c \text{ and } c\leq b  }. $$ We
		call this the closed interval of $a$ and $b$, and if $a=b$ we may
		write $[a]$ instead of $[a,a]$.

label: embedding_lemma
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{embedding_lemma}
	Let $B,B'$ be Boolean algebras, and $e:B\hookrightarrow B'$ an embedding
	of Boolean algebras. Then for each homomorphism $H:
	\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B $ with principal variables there  is a
	homomorphism $H': \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B'$  with principal variables
	such that for all formulas $\varphi \in \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}_{\text{PT}^+}$ $$ b\in H(\varphi)
	\quad \text{ if and only if } \quad e(b) \in H'(\varphi).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume $H: \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$ has principal variables. Thus, for all $i$ there
	exists $b_i\in B$ such that $$H(P_i)= \set{ a\in B | a\leq b_i  }.$$ We
	then define $H': \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B'$ as the homomorphism that maps each
	propositional variable $P_i$ to the principal ideal of $e(b_i)$, i.e.,
	$$H'(P_i)= \set{ a'\in B'| a'\leq e(b_i)}.$$
	
	Clearly, $H'$ has principal variables, so what is left to show is that the
	equivalence in the theorem holds for all $b\in B$ and all formulas $\varphi$
	of PT$^+$. In order to do so, we need an additional lemma best described
	using the notation of Boolean intervals.\footnote{The introduction of
	Boolean intervals in this context is inspired by their usage in
	\cite{Hella2023} in which minimal covers of Boolean intervals are used to
	define complexity measures for expressions in first-order team semantics.
	Even if our usage is noticeably different, the proof construction we
	present for forming included covering intervals is strongly related to the
	constructive methods of generating minimal interval covers for collections
	of teams satisfying a formula presented in that paper.}

\begin{claim} 
Let $B$ and $B'$ be Boolean algebras, let $e:B\hookrightarrow B'$ be a Boolean
algebra embedding, let $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}\to {\mathcal P} B$ be a homomorphism, and let
$H':\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}\to {\mathcal P} B'$ be the homomorphism generated from $H$ as described above.
Then, for all $\varphi\in \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}_{\mathrm{PT}^+}$ and all $b'\in B'$, if $b'\in H'
(\varphi)$, then there is some $b\in B$ such that $b'\leq e(b)$ and $[b',e
(b)]\subseteq H'(\varphi)$.
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
	We prove this statement for all $b\in B$ by induction over the complexity
	of formulas. Let $b_i$ denote the generating element of the principal
	ideal $H(P_i)$.
	\begin{itemize}
		\item Assume $\varphi = \mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax}$. Then $b'\in H'(\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax})$ only if $b'=  0
		= e(0)$, and thus $[b', e(0)]= [0] \subseteq H'(\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax})$.
		\item Assume $\varphi = \mathord{\text{NB}} $. Then if $b'\in H'(\mathord{\text{NB}})$ clearly
		$[b',e(1)]\subseteq H'(\mathord{\text{NB}})$.
		\item Assume $\varphi = P_i$. If $b'\in H'(P_i)$, then $b'\leq e(b_i)$
		and, since $H'(P_i)$ is a principal ideal, clearly
		$[b',e(b_i)]\subseteq  H'(P_i)$.
		\item Assume $\varphi = \mathord{{\sim}} P_i $. By Lemma \ref{negated_principal}
		and a similar argument as for the previous case we can conclude that
		if $b'\in H'(\mathord{{\sim}} P_i)$ then $[b', e(- b_i)] \subseteq H'(\mathord{{\sim}}
		P_i)$.
		\item Assume $\varphi = \psi \land \chi$. If $b'\in H'(\varphi)$, then
		$b'\in H'(\psi)$ and $b'\in H'(\chi)$. By induction, we may find
		$b_\psi,b_\chi\in B$ such that $[b',e(b_\psi)]\subseteq H'(\psi)$ and
		$[b',e(b_\chi)]\subseteq H'(\chi)$. Since $e$  is a
		homomorphism $$[b',e(b_\psi \cdot b_\chi)]\subseteq H'(\varphi).$$
		\item $\varphi = \psi \lor \chi$. If $b' \in H'(\varphi)$, then $b'\in
		H'(\psi)$ or $b'\in H'(\chi)$, and without loss of generality we may
		assume the former. By induction hypothesis there is some $b_\psi \in
		B$ such that $[b',e(b_\psi)]\subseteq H'(\psi)$, and thus
		$[b',e(b_\psi)]\subseteq H'(\varphi)$.
		\item $\varphi = \psi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \chi$. If $b'\in H'(\varphi)$, then there is $
		c'+ d'= b'$ such that $c'\in H'(\psi)$ and $d'\in H'(\chi)$. By
		induction hypothesis, we can then find $b_\psi, b_\chi \in B$ such
		that $[c',e(b_\psi)]\subseteq H'(\psi)$ and $[d',e(b_\chi)]\subseteq
		H'(\chi)$. Then since $b'= c'+ d'$ and $e$ is a homomorphism, it is
		easy to see that $$H'(\varphi)\supseteq \set{ p+ q | p\in
		[c',e(b_\psi)], q \in [d', e(b_\chi)]} = [b', e(b_\psi +
		b_\chi)].$$
	\end{itemize}
	This concludes the proof of the claim.
\end{proof}

Now we are ready to finish the proof of the lemma. Again
this is achieved for all $b\in B$ by induction over the complexity of
formulas.
	\begin{itemize}
	\item Assume $\varphi = \mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax}$. First note that $b\in H(\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax})$ if and only
	if $ b= 0\in B$ and  $b'\in H'(\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax})$ if and only if $b'= 0 \in
	B'$. Then note that $e(0)= 0\in B'$ by $e$ being a homomorphism, and
	by $e$ being injective $e(b)= 0$ if and only if $b= 0\in B$. These
	observations suffice to prove the statement.
	\item Assume $\varphi = \mathord{\text{NB}}$. Since regardless of homomorphism and algebra
	$H(\mathord{\text{NB}})$ is the complement set of $H(\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax})$, a similar argument proves
	the statement.
	\item Assume $\varphi = P_i$. For all $b\in B$ we have that  $b\in H({\mathcal P}_i)$
	if and only if $b\leq b_i$. Then by $e$ being an embedding this holds if
	and only if  $e(b)\leq e(b_i)$, which is equivalent to $e(b)\in H'(P_i)$.
	\item Assume $\varphi = \mathord{{\sim}} P_i$. By Lemma \ref{negated_principal}
	$H(\mathord{{\sim}} P_i)$ is the principal ideal generated by $- b_i$. Similarly,
	$H'(\mathord{{\sim}} P_i) $  is the principal ideal generated by $- e(b_i)$.
	Thus, a similar argument as for $\varphi = P_i$ suffices.
	\item Assume $\varphi = \psi \land \chi$. Then $b\in H(\varphi)$ if and only if
	$b\in H(\psi)$ and $b\in H(\chi)$. By induction we can conclude that this
	holds if and only if  $e(b)\in H'(\psi)$ and $e(b)\in H'(\chi)$ which
	holds if and only if  $e(b)\in H'(\varphi)$.
	\item Assume $\varphi = \psi \lor \chi$. The result follows in a similar 
	way as the previous case.
	\item Assume $\varphi = \psi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \chi$. If $b\in H(\varphi)$, then there
	exists $c+ d = b$ such that $c\in H(\psi)$ and $d\in H(\chi)$. By
	induction hypothesis we directly see that $e(b)= e(c)+ e(d) \in
	H'(\varphi)$. For the other direction, assume $e(b)\in H'(\varphi)$. Then there
	exists $c'+ d' = e(b)$ such that $c'\in H'(\psi) $ and $d'\in
	H'(\chi)$. Now by the interval lemma above we can find $b_\psi, b_\chi \in
	B$ such that $[c',e(b_\psi)]\subseteq H'(\psi)$ and
	$[d',e(b_\chi)]\subseteq H'(\chi)$. Now, let $c= b\cdot b_\psi$ then
	$$e(c)= e(b)\cdot e(b_\psi)= (c'+ d')\cdot e(b_\psi)= c'+  (d' \cdot
	e(b_\psi))$$ so that clearly $e(c)\in [c', e(b_\psi)]\subseteq H'(\psi)$,
	and by induction hypothesis $c\in H(\psi)$. Similarly define $d= b\cdot
	b_\chi$ and conclude that $d\in H(\chi)$. 

	What is left to show is that $b=c+ d$. Since
	$c'\leq e(b_\psi)$ and $d'\leq e(b_\chi)$, we have
	\[
		e(b)=c'+ d'
		\leq e(b_\psi)+ e(b_\chi)
		= e(b_\psi+ b_\chi).
	\]
	As $e$ is an embedding, it reflects the order, and hence
	$b\leq b_\psi+ b_\chi$. Therefore,
	\[
		c+ d
		=
		(b\cdot b_\psi)+(b\cdot b_\chi)
		=
		b\cdot(b_\psi+ b_\chi)
		=
		b.
	\]
	Thus $b=c+ d$ with $c\in H(\psi)$ and $d\in H(\chi)$, so
	$b\in H(\psi\mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax}\chi)=H(\varphi)$.
\end{itemize} 
This concludes the proof of the lemma.

label: f_rep_in_Val
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{f_rep_in_Val}
For every Boolean algebra of the form $({\mathcal P} S, \emptyset, \cdot^C, \cup ,\cap)$
and every homomorphism $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} {\mathcal P} S$ with principal
variables there is a mapping $f_H:S \to 2^{\mathbb{N}}$  such that for all
formulas $\varphi \in \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}_{\text{PT}^+}$ and all $X\in {\mathcal P} S$:
\[ 
X\in H(\varphi) \quad \text{iff} \quad f_H^*(X) \in H_V(\varphi),
\] 
where $f_H^*:{\mathcal P} S \to {\mathcal P} 2^{\mathbb{N}}$ is defined by $f_H^*(X) = \set{f_H(x) | x
\in X}$, and $H_V:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P}{\mathcal P} 2^\mathbb{N}$ denotes the valuation
homomorphism.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume $H:\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} {\mathcal P} S$ has principal variables. Let $f: S\to
	2^{\mathbb{N}}$ be defined by
	\[
		f(s)(i)= \begin{cases} 1 & \text{ if } \{s\} \in H(P_i) \\ 
								0 & \text{ if } \{s\} \notin  H(P_i).
					\end{cases}
	\]

	\begin{claim} 
	For all $X,Y\in {\mathcal P} S$, $f^*(X\cup Y) = f^*(X)\cup f^*(Y)$.
	Furthermore, if $f^*(X) = U\cup V$, then there exist $Y,Z\in {\mathcal P} S$ such
	that $f^*(Y)= U$, $f^*(Z)= V$ and $Y\cup Z= X$.
	\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of claim]
	The first part of the claim is self-evident by the definition of $f^*$
	from $f$. For the second part, let $Y= \set{s\in X| f(s)\in U}$ and $Z=
	\set{s\in X | f(s) \in V}$.  Then every element of $X$ belongs to $Y\cup Z$,
	since $f(s)\in f^*(X)=U\cup V$, and by construction we have
	$f^*(Y)=U$ and $f^*(Z)=V$.
\end{proof}	
	We can now prove that the function $f$ is what we looked for in the lemma
	by induction over formulas $\varphi\in	\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}_{\text{PT}^+}$.
	
	We have four types of base cases:  $\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax}, \mathord{\text{NB}}, P_i, \mathord{{\sim}} P_i $:
	\begin{itemize}
		\item Assume $\varphi = \mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax}$. By definition $X\in H(\mathord{\vphantom{\bot}\mathpalette\ibot@\relax})$ iff $X= \emptyset$, and
		since $f^*(X) = \emptyset $ if and only if $X= \emptyset$ this case is evident.
		\item Assume $\varphi = \mathord{\text{NB}}$. This case is proved by contraposition of the previous
		case.
		\item Assume $\varphi = P_i$. By assumption $H(P_i)$ is a principal ideal in the Boolean
		algebra ${\mathcal P} S$. Hence, for all $X \in H(P_i)$, by downward closure we have
		for all $s\in X$ that $\{s\} \in H(P_i)$. By construction then
		$f^*(\{s\}) \in H_V (P_i)$ for all $s\in X$, and thus since $H_V$ has
		principal variables we find that $f^*(X)\in
		H_V(P_i)$. The opposite direction is proved with a similar chain of
		arguments.
		\item Assume $\varphi = \mathord{{\sim}} P_i$. Then by Lemma
		\ref{negated_principal} we assert that for all $H\in \mathcal{H}_{PV}$
		we have that $H(\mathord{{\sim}} P_i)$ is a principal ideal. The proof is then
		similar to the previous case.
	\end{itemize}

	For the induction step we have three cases for the main connectives:
	$\land ,\lor,\mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax}$
	\begin{itemize}
		\item Assume $\varphi = \psi \land \chi$. $X\in H(\varphi)$ by definition if
		and only if $X\in H(\psi)$ and $X\in H(\chi)$. By induction
		hypothesis, we can conclude that is the case if and only if $f^*(X)\in
		H_V(\psi)$ and $f^*(X)\in H_V(\chi)$, which is equivalent to stating
		that $f^*(X) \in H_V(\varphi)$.
		\item Assume $\varphi = \psi \lor \chi$. The proof is similar to the previous case.
		\item Assume  $\varphi = \psi \mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \chi$. For one direction, assume $X \in
		H(\varphi)$. Then there exist $Y\in H(\psi)$ and $Z\in H(\chi)$ such
		that  $X= Y\cup Z$. By induction hypothesis $f^*(Y)\in H_V(\psi)$ and
		$f^*(Z)\in H_V(\chi)$. By the first part of the Claim about $f^*$ we
		see that $f^*(X)= f^*(Y)\cup f^*(Z)$ and thus $f^*(X)\in H_V(\varphi)$.
		
		For the other direction, assume $f^*(X) \in H_V(\varphi)$.  Then there
		exist $U\in H_V(\psi), V\in H_V(\chi)$ such that $f^*(X)=U\cup V$.
		Then by the second part of the Claim about $f^*$, there exists $Z, Y$
		such that $f^*(Z)=U, f^*(Y)= V$ and $Z\cup Y= X$. By the induction
		hypothesis  $Z\in H(\psi)$ and $Y\in H(\chi)$.  We conclude
		that $X\in H(\varphi)$.
	\end{itemize}
	This concludes the proof of the lemma.

title: Proof
body_md:
By applying Theorem \ref{Def_to_ax} the statement of Theorem \ref{thm:mainAx} is equivalent to the statement that for all $\Delta \cup \{
	\varphi \} \subseteq \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}_{\text{PT}^+}$ 
	\[
	\Delta \vDash_{\text{PT}^+} \varphi \quad \text{iff} \quad
	\Delta \vDash_{\mathcal{H}_{\text{PV}}} \varphi.
	\]
	The right-to-left direction follows directly from Proposition \ref{directThm} and the fact
	that $H_V\in\mathcal{H}_{\text{PV}} $. 

	The other direction is proved by contraposition. Assume
	$\mathcal{H}_{\text{PV}} :  \Delta \nvDash \varphi$ and thus  $\text{LTP} :
	\text{PVA}, \Delta \nvDash \varphi$.  Then there is some Boolean algebra $B$ and 
	homomorphism $H: \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to  {\mathcal P} B$ such that $ H:
	\text{PVA},\Delta \nvDash \varphi.$ In other words, $H\in
	\mathcal{H}_{\text{PV}}$ and there exists an element $ b\in B $ such that
	\[
	b \in \bigcap_{\delta\in \Delta} H(\delta), \text{ but } b \notin H(\varphi).
	\]  
	By Theorem \ref{thm:completeBA}, we can then find an embedding $e :B \hookrightarrow {\mathcal P}{S}$ of $B$ into a complete atomic Boolean algebra of the form $({\mathcal P} S, \emptyset, \cdot^C, \cup
	,\cap)$. Then by Lemma \ref{embedding_lemma} and \ref{f_rep_in_Val}  we can find a homomorphism $H':\ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}\to {\mathcal P}{\mathcal P} S$, and a mapping $f_{H'}: S\to 2^\mathbb{N}$  such that 
	\[
	f_{H'}^*(e(b)) \in \bigcap_{\delta\in\Delta} H_V(\delta), \text{ but }
	f_{H'}^*(e(b))\notin H_V(\varphi).
	\]
	Thus, $H_V :\Delta \nvDash \varphi$ and by Theorem \ref{directThm}: 
	\[
	\Delta \nvDash_{\text{PT}^+} \varphi.
	\] 
	This finalises the proof of Theorem	\ref{thm:mainAx}.

label: lem: strict not props
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: strict not props} For all Boolean algebras $B$ and all $A\in {\mathcal P} B$:
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item $b \in \mathord{{\sim}} A$ if and only if $- b$ is an upper bound of $A$.
		\item $b\in \mathord{{\sim}}  A$ if and only if $\phantom{-}b$ is a\phantom{n} lower bound of $A^{-}= \set{- a |a\in  A}$.
		\item	$ \mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} A$ is the set of lower bounds of the upper bounds of $A$, that is 
		$$ \mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} A = \set{b | b\leq c \text{ for all }  c  \text{ such that } a\leq c \text { for all } a\in A}, $$ 
		\item $\mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}}  A$ is a principal ideal if and only if $\bigvee A$ exists in  $B$.
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
~
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item 
		First assume $b\in \mathord{{\sim}} A$. Then $b\cdot a = 0$ for all $a\in A$, and thus
		$$a= a\cdot (b+- b)=  0 + (a\cdot - b)= a\cdot - b$$
		This holds for all $a \in A$ and thus $- b$ is an upper bound of $A$.
		
		For the other direction, assume $- b$ is an upper bound of $A$. Then for all $a\in A$ 
		$$a =a \cdot ( b + - b) = (a\cdot b)  + (a \cdot - b)= (a \cdot b) + a,$$ 
		proving that $a\cdot  b \leq  a$. Since $-b$ is an upper bound for all $a$ we also conclude $$(a\cdot b) \leq (a\cdot b)\cdot - b= 0.$$  Thus, for all $a\in A$ we have that  $  a\cdot b = 0$ proving that $ b \in \mathord{{\sim}} A$.
		\item 
		Observe that if $a\leq b$ for all $a\in A$, then $- b \leq - a$ for all $a\in A$, proving that $b$ is a lower bound for $A^-$ exactly when $- b$ is an upper bound for $A$.
		\item Follows directly from (1) and (2):
		$$\mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} A= \set{b| b\leq c\text{ for all } c \in \set{ - d | d\in \mathord{{\sim}} A} }$$ 
		$$= \set{b| b\leq c\text{ for all } c \in \set{ - d | a\leq - d \text { for all } a\in A} }$$ 
		$$= \set{b | b\leq c \text{ for all }  c \text{ such that } a\leq c \text { for all } a\in A}.$$
		\item
			First assert that if a least upper bound of a set $A$ exists it is equivalent to the least upper bound of the lower bounds of the upper bounds of the set. By (3) we can thus conclude that $\bigvee A= \bigvee \mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} A$ and that they exist simultaneously. 
			Assume $\dot{a} =  \bigvee A$ exists in  $B$. Then $\dot{a}$ is a lower bound of all upper bounds of $A$, and by (3) $\dot{a}\in \mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} A$ and $\mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} A= \set{ b | b\leq \dot{a}}$ is a principal ideal. On the other hand, assuming $\mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} A$ is a principal ideal, then there is some $c\in \mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} A$ such that $d\leq c$ for all $d\in \mathord{{\sim}}\mathord{{\sim}} A$. Clearly then $c= \bigvee \mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} A$ and thus $\bigvee A$ exists in $B$.
	\end{enumerate}

label: negation elim
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{negation elim} 
	For all Boolean algebras $B$, all homomorphisms $ H: \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}} \to {\mathcal P} B$, and all
	formulas $\varphi \in \ensuremath{\mathtt{Fm}}$ we have $$ \vDash_H \mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} \varphi \to \varphi
	\quad \text{iff}\quad \mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} H(\varphi)= H(\varphi). $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition \ref{prop_strict_neg} (1) and the substitutionality of LTP, we
have that $\vDash \varphi\to \mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} \varphi$ and it is clear that the
proposition follows from how $\to$ and $\mathord{{\sim}}$ are defined.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
For all atomic formulas  $P$, we have in LTP that $$\Box
	(\mathord{{\sim}} \mathord{{\sim}} P \to P)\nvDash \Box (P\mathrel{\vphantom{\lor}\mathpalette\ilor@\relax} \mathord{{\sim}} P ).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{lem: strict not props} (4) together with Theorem \ref
	{excluded_middle} and Proposition \ref{negation elim} it is clear that
	any non-complete Boolean algebra serves as a counterexample to the
	entailment.
